clue.text: Edward's of Islamic faith, Spooner tells us, and is visibly moved

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words as he talked, so naming him is the whole instruction.

parts.note: Ted is the everyday short form of Edward
the Shia are one of the two great branches of Islam
say those three words with the opening sounds of the first and last traded, T for SH

explanation.walkthrough: A spoonerism is easiest solved from the definition end: think of the phrase for weeping, trade its opening sounds back, and the clue's picture of Edward appears. Everyman always names the reverend so you know to try it.
explanation.definitionFit: To shed a tear is to weep just enough for it to show, so the phrase covers being moved in a way onlookers can see.

clue.text: Lays the ground for irritating types

definitions.meaning: turf arrives as cut squares of earth and grass, and laying them over bare soil is a groundsman's job
mild British abuse for an annoying person, printable enough for a Sunday paper

explanation.walkthrough: Two plain senses laid side by side with 'for' as the only join. The gardening one is the one that hides: a lawn is laid in squares, and the verb comes straight off the noun for a square.
explanation.definitionFit: A sod is a cut square of turf, so laying them is turfing a lawn; the same word is mild British abuse for an annoying person.

clue.text: Bovary? A Madame that's written about?

indicators.note: About means round, and a thing set down the other way round arrives back to front, so the pieces are read from the far end.

parts.note: the indefinite article, taken at face value as a single letter
Mme is the standard French abbreviation for Madame, as printed on an envelope

explanation.walkthrough: The italics sell you a novel title, and the definition really is its heroine, named by her surname alone. The wordplay treats the same word as a scrap of everyday French correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaubert's Madame Bovary is Emma Bovary, so the surname defines the answer only as an example of the woman who bears it.

clue.text: Prediction: more food will lead to fight not starting

indicators.note: Whatever leads goes in front, so the first chunk is written down and the second falls in behind it.
A word that is not starting has given up the letter it begins with, and only the remainder is used.

parts.note: a second helping at the table is called seconds
the word for a scrap, without the F it begins with

explanation.walkthrough: The colon is doing the work of an equals sign. On the surface a canteen queue turns nasty; the definition is the fairground gift of knowing what happens next.
explanation.definitionFit: Second sight is the claimed power of foreseeing events, so it stands for prediction as the faculty rather than a single forecast.

clue.text: Traffic; perhaps old vehicle

definitions.meaning: to traffic in something is to deal in it, buying and selling
the car you hand the garage counts against the price of the new one

explanation.walkthrough: The semicolon is the join. One half is a verb about dealing, the other the noun a dealer uses, and 'perhaps' concedes that a car is only one of the things you can hand over.
explanation.definitionFit: To traffic in goods is to trade in them, and what you trade in at a garage is the old car itself, which is why 'perhaps' is there.

clue.text: Mixed gin in English ceremonial county — or somewhere in Provence

indicators.note: A mixed drink has had its contents stirred together, so the letters beside the word will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: Avon, centred on Bristol and Bath, was an English county until 1996 and still names the area's police and fire services
the three letters of the drink, stirred and then dropped into the middle of the county

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman keeps the surface thoroughly English, a measure of gin and a shire, and lands the definition in the south of France. 'Ceremonial county' is the signal that a place name is wanted as letters rather than as a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Avignon is a walled city on the Rhone in Provence, famous for its papal palace and its half-finished bridge.

clue.text: Mark and Cliff

definitions.meaning: the line a healed wound leaves behind on skin
a bare rock face on a northern English fell, a word that turns up all over Yorkshire place names

explanation.walkthrough: Two capital letters do all the misleading: Mark and Cliff read as a pair of blokes, and neither is a name here. The second sense is landscape English rather than dictionary English.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is both the mark a wound leaves on skin and, in northern hill country, a cliff of bare exposed rock.

clue.text: Prosaic echinus every so often removed: that's somewhat whimsical

indicators.note: Every so often means at intervals rather than continuously, so letters are taken from every other place in the word and not from all of them.
This does two jobs at once: the letters at the skipped places are taken away, and what survives is removed from its old order too, which is the loosest link in the clue.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, handed over whole
the second, fourth and sixth letters of the zoologist's name for a sea urchin, the other four dropped

explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' reads like a marker for something buried in the clue's letters, and that is the false trail; it only softens the definition. The whole misdirection sits in an unfamiliar name for a common seaside creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Capricious means governed by sudden whims, so 'whimsical' is the plain synonym and 'somewhat' only softens it a little.

clue.text: Wrongfully arrest and hear certain elements

indicators.note: Something done wrongfully has not been done properly, and letters handled improperly come out in an order nobody intended.

parts.note: six letters of fodder
four more, joined on by the clue's own 'and'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrongfully arrest' is a complete news headline, which is why the fodder hides so well. The elements themselves are neither particularly rare nor earths, but the chemists' name stuck.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare earths are the seventeen metallic elements, the lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium, used in magnets and phone screens.

clue.text: Comic rated 'poor' as the public chooses

indicators.note: A verdict of poor says the thing was badly put together, and badly put together is what happens to these ten letters.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, the two words run together

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the giveaway. The reviewer's verdict is the instruction, while the word immediately before it is material, and 'a comic rated poor' is a perfectly ordinary sentence meaning none of that.
explanation.definitionFit: A decision made democratically is settled by the vote of everyone, which is precisely the whole public doing the choosing.

clue.text: Pole and box

definitions.meaning: a length of timber or metal holding up a ship's sails
to trade practice punches in the ring rather than fight in earnest

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P offers a nationality and 'box' offers a container; neither reading survives. One noun and one verb, sharing a spelling and nothing else.
explanation.definitionFit: A spar is a ship's mast or boom, and to spar is to box for practice: one noun and one verb with no connection between them.

clue.text: Love disposing of Chilean wine now and again

indicators.note: To dispose things is to arrange them, so this asks for a fresh arrangement rather than, as it looks, for something to be thrown away.

parts.note: love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as a zero
eleven letters of fodder, which with the tennis score make the twelve wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Love disposing of' reads as getting rid of the O, and that is the trap. Dispose here is the tidy-minded sense, arrange, so the O joins the shuffle instead of leaving it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms for something that happens at irregular intervals, neither often nor never, and they swap in for each other exactly.

clue.text: Where to go in castle tower undergoing restoration

indicators.note: A building under restoration is taken apart and put back together, which is what happens to the eleven letters in front of the phrase.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder, no letter wasted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface stays with the builders while the definition slips into the euphemism a parent uses to a child. WC on a British door or floor plan is short for exactly this phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A water closet is the formal name for a lavatory, so 'where to go' is the polite English way of asking for one.

clue.text: M.O.s involving secure drop

indicators.note: Something involved is tangled up rather than straight, so the letters beside the word are wound into a new order.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder

explanation.walkthrough: M.O. is police-drama shorthand for modus operandi, Latin for way of operating. 'Secure drop' sounds like spy tradecraft, which is why the letters sit there unexamined.
explanation.definitionFit: An M.O. is a modus operandi, the settled way somebody goes about a job, which is what one of these is.

clue.text: Current events — or, figuratively, the public's responses

definitions.meaning: movements of the sea driven by the pull of the tide, arriving all at once
when a whole country reacts together, the reaction is pictured as water sweeping everything before it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Current events' is deliberately the newsreader's phrase and is nothing of the sort: the currents are in the sea. The second half admits with 'figuratively' that it is only a metaphor.
explanation.definitionFit: Waves driven by tides are events made of currents, and a sudden mass of public feeling is described with the same picture of oncoming water.

clue.text: Checks score in Singapore when some are ignored

indicators.note: The letters at each end of the phrase are the ones being passed over, and what nobody ignores is the unbroken run left in the middle.

parts.note: seven letters running consecutively across the three words, beginning part-way into the first

explanation.walkthrough: 'Checks score' reads as one phrase about a scoreboard, which is the misdirection: the split falls after the very first word, and the rest of the clue is the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: To rein in a horse is to pull it up short, so the phrase means holding something back, which is what checking an impulse does.

clue.text: Increasingly deranged old teachers having row

parts.note: the National Union of Teachers, a British union that existed until it merged into a larger one in 2017, hence 'old'
a row of seats set one above another, as in a theatre

explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises a staffroom argument, and 'row' is the pivot: read as a quarrel it goes nowhere, read as a line of seats it pays.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutty is slang for mad, so its comparative says somebody is madder than before rather than simply mad.

clue.text: Chirpy haphazard assistant that'll give plausibleish text, primarily?

definitions.text: Chirpy haphazard assistant that'll give plausibleish text, primarily?

indicators.note: In the first place is what primarily means, so each word ahead of it surrenders only the character it opens with.

parts.words: Chirpy haphazard assistant that'll give plausibleish text
parts.note: seven words standing in a row, each handing over the letter it begins with

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the sentence is both the description and the recipe, so nothing is left over. 'Plausibleish' is the joke — confident, fluent and not necessarily right.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes the chatbot itself: an eager, unpredictable helper that turns out text reading plausibly whether or not it is true.

clue.text: Rubbish comprising uneaten peach parts?

definitions.meaning: in British English, calling something rubbish means it is dreadful, the worst of its kind
the hard stone at the centre of the fruit is the bit that goes in the bin

explanation.walkthrough: The definite article belongs to the idiom rather than to the fruit: peaches supply pits, and only 'the pits' means dreadful. The question mark admits that treating the stones this way is playful.
explanation.definitionFit: The stone of a peach is its pit, and 'the pits' is the idiom, American-born and now everyday British slang, for the very worst of anything.

clue.text: Cast can be heard from beginning to end

indicators.note: What can only be heard reaches you as a sound and not a spelling, so what gets written down is the other word that sounds the same.

parts.note: to cast a stone is to throw it, and cast is already a past tense, so the word said aloud is the past tense too

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like the theatrical noun and is a verb, and specifically a past tense — that is what makes the sound land. Everyman's 'can be heard' is a homophone marker in plain clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Reading a book through means covering it from first page to last, so the word carries the whole of something end to end.

clue.text: Journey arriving at oil rig regularly somewhere in Libya

indicators.note: What a journey arrives at comes after the journey, so the second chunk is written in behind the first.

parts.note: a short journey is a trip

indicators.note: Something done regularly happens at fixed intervals, so letters are picked at every other place instead of one after another.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of the two words run together

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sends you offshore to an oil worker's commute and the answer is in North Africa. 'Regularly' is easy to read as scenery — a rig visited regularly — when it is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is Libya's capital and chief port on the Mediterranean, so the country named points at the city inside it.

clue.text: As trolleys and some trains proceed?

definitions.text: As trolleys and some trains proceed?

parts.note: the surface offers a supermarket, where a trolley is pushed along the gangway between the shelves
the trains the setter means are not railway ones but the trailing part of a bride's dress, which proceeds at walking pace

explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay to find, only two senses of 'train' — the railway sort with a gangway down the middle, and the sort a wedding dress has. Both go the same way to get where they are going.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the walk a bride makes to the altar, and a shop trolley runs along the same kind of gangway between rows.

clue.text: College official having stripped off on retirement denied knighthood

indicators.note: Something that retires goes back the way it came, so the letters are read from the far end instead of the near one.
What is denied you never arrives, so the letter it points at is left out of the assembly altogether.

parts.note: somebody who has stripped off is naked, and the word is written out before anything is done to it
a knighthood shows as K in the honours list, as in KBE and KCMG, and that K is the letter dropped here

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a scandal in the senior common room. 'Denied knighthood' sounds like a career ruined and is one letter refused, which is Everyman's joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A dean heads a faculty, or at Oxford and Cambridge keeps discipline in a college, so the office is an official one exactly as described.

clue.text: Spot of land grabbed from Murmansk yesterday

indicators.note: What is grabbed from something is lifted out of it as it stands, unaltered, so the letters come away in the order they were sitting in.

parts.note: four consecutive letters bridging the gap between the two words, two coming from each

explanation.walkthrough: A Russian port and a plain adverb, put together because the join between them is where the island sits. 'Spot of land' is vague on purpose: it could be a field, a farm or a stain on a map.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland, and an island is a spot of land in a sea.

clue.text: After drop of Riesling (round #5), Everyman's beginning to ramble

indicators.note: It puts everything that follows behind the piece it names, so the wine supplies the letter at the front.
A word's beginning is the character it starts with, and none of the rest of the name is wanted.
A drop of a drink is the smallest measure of it, and the smallest measure of a written word is the first letter of the name.

parts.note: the first letter of the German white wine's name
a round shape drawn on the page is the letter O
the hash sign means number, and five as a Roman numeral is V
the setter signs his own puzzle and only his initial is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman writes himself into his clues most weeks, so his name in a clue is nearly always one letter. The bracket is the tricky part: a hash makes 5 a number, and a number wants Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: To rove is to wander about with no fixed route, which is what rambling over the hills amounts to.

clue.text: Women's group talk including stock index and what may resemble recession

indicators.note: To include something is to have it inside you, so the letters named next go into the gap in the middle rather than on the end.

parts.note: the Women's Institute, the long-established British organisation of countrywomen
the Dow Jones average, the New York market's headline index
a plain synonym, five letters

explanation.walkthrough: Every money word is misdirection: the recession here is a hairline in retreat, not an economy shrinking. The name comes from an old superstition that the shape foretold early widowhood.
explanation.definitionFit: A widow's peak is the V of hair pointing down the forehead, and its shape mimics a hairline receding, which is recession as hair rather than economics.

clue.text: Frame small tree

parts.note: S is the clothes-label abbreviation for small
a common British hardwood, three letters

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, no indicator, no joinery: the shortest kind of charade there is. 'Frame' is the window sense, not a picture's or a boxer's.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is the wooden frame holding the panes in a sash window, the part that slides up and down in its box.

clue.text: Nitwit with one point of view: some help!

parts.note: an ass is a fool, the donkey pressed into service as an insult
the Roman numeral for one
the position you take on a question is your stance

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells 'some help!' as sarcasm aimed at the nitwit, and that is the misdirection — it is the straight definition. I for one is the commonest single letter in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Assistance is help as an uncountable noun, the aid given rather than one act of it, which is why 'some' sits comfortably in front.
